When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.
“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”

But despite households’ surge in interest in cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to be slashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget.
Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging,” he said.


“Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.”
The boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers.
Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a “critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn


President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events




Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US faces a cascade of hazards fueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter.
From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, canceling contracts and grants, and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting, has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025.

The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices.

The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has plummeted morale, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps.


“The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central.
That test could soon be coming.
This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.
Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, land slides and flash floods.
“Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said.
Noaa plays a pivotal role in public safety and provides key insights and forecasts relied upon by a vast array of communities and industries, from weather shifts that could affect crop schedules, to emergency response preparations when hurricanes are brewing or fire conditions are aligning

Andy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said.
Big decisions on North Sea drilling, the expansion of Heathrow airport, electric vehicles (EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers.

Super-rich get ‘double dividend’ from causes and costs of climate crisis, report finds


Oxfam says investing by rich in disaster recovery widens inequality and gives incentive to delay climate action




The world’s wealthiest people are not just profiting from the polluting causes of climate breakdown, they are also increasingly cashing in on the catastrophic consequences, according to a study by Oxfam.
The global equality organisation has found that the richest 0.1% of the world’s population are heavily invested in disaster preparedness, recovery and reconstruction – a market that is projected to grow from $70bn to $92bn a year by 2029.

This gives the planet’s wealthiest and most powerful people a “double dividend” from the climate crisis and, more alarmingly, an incentive to delay or disrupt action to solve the problem, the NGO says.
It also worsens global inequality as those least responsible for global heating end up having to pay those most responsible in terms of higher food prices, repairing homes damaged by extreme weather or relocating to other areas.


Jean McLean, Oxfam’s chief influencing officer, accused billionaires of turning chaos into profit. “The super-rich benefit at both ends of the crisis: first, through continued investment in polluting industries, and second, through investment in the booming ‘adaptation economy’ – recovery and rebuilding services are sold back to a warming world,” she said.
“The populations who contributed least to the climate crisis are absorbing its worst consequences, while those who caused it are best equipped to protect themselves.”
The richest 0.1% on the planet, a group of 8 million people, are responsible for more carbon emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion combined, the report says. As a result, this group have reportedly contributed by 125 times more than the average person to extreme heat events.
This is partly due to lifestyles. The world’s private jets, for example, release more CO2 in two seconds than most of the world’s people emit in an entire year. But the biggest impact of this group comes from their investments.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days
articles.raw_rss: From Brexit debates to North Sea oil, there is plenty getting the cabinet, the Labour Party and the country talking.

articles.jina_text:
It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet. 
Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.
Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.
First up, the Budget
You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week. 
There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.
But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.














Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.
Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.
You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.
Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU
In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.
Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.
Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.
On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum. 










Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.

UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’


V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand 
 
 
Business live – latest updates  




Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers.
Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.

The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand.
If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.


The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job.
Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off.
However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.
Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known as bidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets.
The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could mean an additional 147m tonnes of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by 2050.


Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, a thinktank tracking the transition to electric cars, said: “Vehicle to grid is exciting technology that could help balance the grid and cut bills, but carmakers should only be rewarded if it’s actually used, not just for fitting it.

A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor, John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project.

The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.

The production has taken four years to complete and marks a special milestone as Sir David Attenborough provides narration during his centenary year.








The dolphin, christened Gambara from an Aboriginal term meaning clever, was filmed employing this sophisticated hunting strategy in the shallow waters off Shark Bay in Western Australia.
The discovery represents one of several previously unrecorded ocean behaviours captured across six episodes of the new series.

The hunting method involves the dolphin inserting sponges into specific openings within the coral structure, eliminating potential escape routes for fish she targets.
Director Yoland Bosiger revealed the production team received intelligence about this particular dolphin from a local observer who had witnessed the behaviour in exceptionally transparent, shallow conditions.
"We called her Gambara after the Aboriginal word for clever," Ms Bosiger explained. "She is incredibly good at hunting with a sponge and we think she's probably 40 years old."
The dolphin's unique dorsal fin markings enabled the crew to track her movements using aerial drone technology.





A bottlenose dolphin features in the BBC's Blue Planet III | 
PA









Ms Bosiger also developed what she termed a "stone fish camera" — functioning as submerged surveillance equipment — to document the unprecedented behaviour. "I still can't believe we got it to be honest," she added.
Series producer Lara Bickerton became tearful upon hearing Sir David's voiceover work for the first time, describing the experience as deeply moving given it was her initial collaboration with the broadcaster.
"It's the first time I've worked with Sir David, so I did cry the first time I heard the first line of the Seasonal Seas episode," she admitted. "That was just a dream, to be able to work with him on the show."
Executive producer Liz White emphasised the uncertainty surrounding Sir David's participation, noting his centenary year added particular significance to his involvement. "Obviously there was no guarantee he was going to do it, but the fact it's his 100th year as well makes it feel so much more special to us," she said.

Full SummaryThe Bank of England warns that this year’s exceptionally strong El Niño could gradually push up UK food prices and possibly influence interest rates, prompting both monetary authorities and the UK government to use climate forecasts for anticipatory action and financial risk management.
This year’s El Niño, the natural weather phenomenon that drives variations in temperature and winds across the Pacific, has prompted the UK government to pledge £15 million to help vulnerable countries such as Malawi, Kenya and Zambia prepare for droughts, floods and food shortages.
But the UK’s economic response will go beyond international aid. The Bank of England has identified El Niño as one of the key factors that could increase food inflation in 2027.
This connection between a climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean and supermarket prices (and possibly interest rates) in the UK is a clear demonstration of how extreme weather is an economic issue as well as an environmental one.





Environmentally speaking, the effects of El Niño can be devastating, bringing severe drought to some regions and severe flooding to others. And a stronger El Niño has a larger influence on global weather patterns than a weaker one.
This year’s event, already the strongest on record, is expected to peak later this year, and could cause global economic problems if it has a negative effect on major agricultural producers or transport routes.

articles.raw_rss: Conservation groups say black poplars are endangered due to felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
articles.raw_meta: Conservation groups say black poplars are endangered due to felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
articles.jina_text:
Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain.
Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently.
Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth.
The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise £20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites.
Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to £10,000.
Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects.














Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back.
He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover".

articles.jina_text:
An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.









The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.









But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.









Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.



Tanker hit 14 days ago




BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.

articles.jina_text:
Across the US west, rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat to the point of vanishing. About 300 glaciers have disappeared since the 1960s, with almost all of the rest set to drastically shrink as the climate crisis continues to escalate, a new study has found.
At the midpoint of the last century more than 1,450 glaciers – large tongues of ice, snow and rock that move under their own weight and gravity – were threaded throughout the mountains of the American west, providing cool water for ecosystems and agriculture as they gradually melted.







Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn

Read more
Some, in the Sierra Nevada of California, were formed a few thousand years ago while others, such as those in the Pacific north-west, are remnants from even further back in the last ice age, which ended about 11,700 years ago.
The long stories of these perennial masses of ice are coming to a rapid end, however, due to global heating caused by the burning of fossil fuels. The total area of glaciers in the US west has shrunk by a third since the 1960s, the new research found, with evidence this loss is speeding up as temperatures continue to rise.
About 300 of these glaciers have functionally disappeared, meaning they have reduced to the size of about two football fields and no longer move. After dominating mountaintops for thousands of years, hundreds of once regal glaciers have been reduced to tiny, sad scraps of ice just within the span of time since the Beatles released their first record.
“When I realized this it was like, ‘Yikes – that’s a lot more than I thought,’” said Andrew Fountain, a geographer at Portland State University and lead author of the new study.

The US’s largest glaciers are still found in Alaska but Fountain said he wanted to conduct the first proper inventory of the “unloved” glaciers that sit closest to where people live, in the lower 48 states. The new research, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, used satellite data and aerial photography to chart how glaciers across six western US states have receded.
Smaller, south-facing glaciers have experienced the greatest rates of shrinkage, particularly those at lower elevations of below 9,000ft in the Sierra Nevada and under 6,000ft in the Cascade range, which runs along the Pacific north-west.
But even many of the larger glaciers are set to disappear in the next half century, previous work by Fountain has found, with the end of the century likely to see them only existing, in a diminished state, atop the tallest mountains in the west such as Mount Hood and Mount Rainier.

Full SummaryA potentially record‑breaking El Niño this year may boost the odds of wetter, stormier weather and cold snaps in the UK, though its direct impact there remains uncertain.
This year’s El Niño could be unprecedented in strength and “off the charts” of what has been seen in the last four decades, the head of the UN weather agency has warned. 
El Niño is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that occurs when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5°C above the long-term average. 
This can have significant effects on weather around the world, historically increasing the risk of floods, extreme heat, storms and drought.





The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to record levels during October through December, “reflecting the strengthening of El Niño”.

El Niño impacts are already being felt
El Niño’s weather impacts tend to be most severe in regions such as India, East Asia, South America, parts of Africa and the West Pacific.

articles.raw_content:
Whether you’ve stocked up on canned food, or gone further with solar panels and rainwater harvesting, more and more of us are following the government’s advice to get prepared for national emergencies. For those who are less confident about self-sufficiency, a growing range of “prepper” kits are becoming available that promise to include everything you need in an emergency.



Some experts say buying branded kits can be a costly mistake, and most households are far better served by good, ordinary items they’ll actually use, and sometimes already own.





Darren Rhodes, the founder of UK Prepper Hub, has over 40 years of practical experience in emergency planning, risk management and household preparedness. He says a basic emergency kit is no different from having insurance: you hope you never need it, but you’ll be grateful if you do.



Rhodes, who prefers realistic, non-alarmist preparedness strategies for everyday households, has conducted over 100 honest kit reviews – here is a selection of essential items he recommends:

A possible three tornados wallop Arizona, bringing golf-ball sized hail


Violent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and trees and carried thunder and heavy winds through state




Yet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four Corners region surveyed blown-away roofs, trees knocked on to homes and power lines downed from overnight tornadoes that injured one person.
The injuries weren’t life-threatening but rare for an area better known for scalding heat. But this fall has been unusually soggy in the south-west with El Niño conditions that have sent one tropical system after another in from the Pacific, causing the Grand Canyon and surrounding deserts to rage with floods.

Now, golf ball-size hail and tornadoes have joined the mix. National Weather Service meteorologists suspect at least three tornadoes touched down as storms swept across central Arizona late Wednesday.
The nasty weather hit during Lenna Landy’s yoga routine in Overgaard, a community of about 3,000 people 140 miles (225km) north-east of Phoenix. Landy had ignored alerts about a possible tornado, but then the storm struck.
“It was like Zeus-was-angry kind of level, of thunder cracks,” Landy said.
The power went off, her house shook and Landy couldn’t find her glasses.
“If this is my end, I won’t see it coming,” she recalled thinking. “The scariest part was just like, how quickly it came on.”
The storm peeled off nearby roofs, shattered windows and blew a shed into a home, she said. A spruce tree in her yard was split in half.


View image in fullscreen
A storm dumps heavy rain and hail across Flagstaff, Arizona, on Wednesday. Photograph: Cheyanne Mumphrey/AP


Still more severe weather, including large hail, struck Thursday with much of Arizona under tornado and flood watches. Similar weather soaked New Mexico, while swathes of Utah and Colorado were under flood watches and warnings.
Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming in from the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.

Tornadoes are somewhat but not exceptionally unusual in Arizona. Notable outbreaks happened in 2019 and 2010.

Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.

Which reef systems are classified as critically endangered?
 

Almost every coral reef ecosystem on the planet is at high risk of collapse by 2075, a global assessment released on Thursday has found, with warming oceans and heat waves the main drivers.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature announced the findings on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity conference in Albania. It said some 96% of shallow-water reef systems are already critically endangered and could disappear by 2075.
The Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment, the first of its kind, was led scientifically by Mishal Gudka.





“The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair,” said Gudka. “Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events. Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”
The study covered 127 tropical and subtropical ecoregions, taking in 72,726 square miles (188,362 square kilometers) of coral reefs globally. It named climate change the “single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide.”

Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises


Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state




Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.

Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.


“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.
“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.

People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.
The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.
Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.

Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.
About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.

Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.

Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.

“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at CORDIO (Coral Reef Degradation in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.


“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”
The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.

New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill




Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study.
The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.

Conducted using acoustic sonar, multi-depth trawling nets and genetic studies, the study revealed dramatic population drops across the gulf between 2011 and 2015: fish declined by 63.5%, macrocrustaceans including shrimp and krill fell by 62% – severely affecting a primary food source for whales – and cephalopods such as squid and octopus dropped by 59.7%.


Researchers found that the post-spill population crash outpaced any decline recorded in similar waters over the past 60 years. They also noted that natural factors like temperature, oxygen and food availability did not vary with the decline, confirming the spill as the primary cause.
The marine species most severely affected were also among the most vital to open-ocean ecosystems and global food webs. Krill, a primary food source for deep-sea fish and shrimp, plunged by 72.8%. Bristlemouths – likely the most abundant backboned animals on Earth – fell by 69%. Meanwhile, lanternfishes, which sustain seabirds, dolphins, sharks and commercial fisheries, dropped by 62.9%. A 2023 survey of the area found that many of these populations have not recovered sustainably.
Because large amounts of marine species were instantly killed or affected due to chemicals stored in their eggs, this led to sharp reductions in population sizes, in turn leading to reduced genetic variations, the study found.

The world’s coral reef ecosystems almost all face a high risk of collapse in the next 50 years mostly due to warming oceans and heat waves, according to a global assessment released Thursday.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s assessment, announced on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity conference in Albania, found that 96% of shallow-water reef systems are already critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. 
Most of the world’s famous reef systems — including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Coral Triangle in the Western Pacific Ocean and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System and the Red Sea coral reefs — are all critically endangered, the highest level of threat.





“The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, the scientific lead of the global IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment, the first of its kind.
“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” he said. “Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”

The Cali Fund, set up to raise $1bn a year for biodiversity from drug companies, remains near empty




Big pharmaceutical companies have been accused of “free-riding on nature”, after a landmark biodiversity fund that invites businesses to put some of their profits back into conservation was left virtually empty.
The Cali Fund set out to raise $1bn (£750m) annually, by asking companies that profit from nature’s genetics to contribute towards conservation in low-income countries. But more than 18 months after the fund was launched, it remains far below this target.

As of Monday, at the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia, the fund had received just $10,656 in commitments, of which $7,085 had been deposited.
No money has so far been given by major pharmaceutical companies, despite the industry’s reliance on genetic information from organisms around the globe for the development of lucrative new medicines.
The industry’s participation could prove pivotal to the fund’s success. A study by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA) found the top 15 pharmaceutical companies could have contributed $756m based on their performance last year, if they had followed guidelines set out by the fund, which suggests companies make a voluntary contribution of 1% of their profits or 0.1% of revenue.
In 2025, the top 15 pharmaceutical companies generated about $161bn in profits, according to ZCA’s research.
“Look at how much profit these pharmaceutical companies are getting – and we’re only asking for a tiny percentage,” said June Rubis of Macquarie University, who is an Indigenous peoples and local communities representative from Asia and sits on the Cali Fund’s steering committee.
“Definitely, they’re free-riding” on nature, said Rubis, who added that businesses did not appear to recognise the importance of protecting nature or of supporting “communities who have been in the frontlines of defending biodiversity conservation and therefore their future profits”.
The Cali Fund is a key issue to be discussed at the UN biodiversity conference – Cop17 – in Yerevan, this week, and is part of wider efforts to plug a $700bn gap in funding for nature conservation.
At least half of the money from the Cali Fund will be directed towards areas identified as priorities by Indigenous peoples and local communities.

When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.



It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to record levels during October through December, “reflecting the strengthening of El Niño”.

Full SummaryUN scientists warn that, under current policies, global warming could reach 2.8 °C by 2100, with only modest reductions from existing nationally determined contributions, and stress that rapid, deep emissions cuts are needed to limit warming to near‑1.5 °C.
UN scientists have found that, under current climate policies across the world, global warming could reach 2.8C this century and continue to rise thereafter.
The warning came in the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) annual “Emissions Gap” report, released on Wednesday.
The world is set to pass the key threshold of 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels, worsening the risks of climate change.





In the Wednesday report, the UNEP outlined different 1.5C overshoot scenarios, which included a projection suggesting global warming could break 2.8C before 2100.
Nations’ current climate plans, called nationally determined contributions (NDCs), would only reduce emissions by 5-8 per cent by 2030 and 11- 15 per cent by 2035, relative to 2025 levels, the report detailed.

The first storm of the autumn has been named as Storm Austen, with the warning coming into force from 3am until 10am on Friday for Cornwall and parts of Devon. 



An amber weather warning for wind has been issued across Cornwall and Devon, with the Met Office issuing a risk to life from large waves and strong gales.





Further parts of England and South Wales are under a yellow weather warning, with damage to buildings and transport networks probable, along with the possibility of power cuts.

Jackdaw is the name given to a gas field in the North Sea, around 150 miles west of Aberdeen. 
In discussions around drilling for fossil fuels, it’s often paired with an oil field called Rosebank, because both of these large projects were backed by the Tories before being blocked by a court ruling. 
Due to the ruling, the companies behind the ventures had to pull together extra information about their predicted climate impact before resubmitting their applications. 
Jackdaw is typically seen as less controversial than Rosebank, because it would supply gas for British homes while Rosebank would produce oil to be exported for the global market. 
 
   
Shell and Norway’s state oil company Equinor are jointly responsible for Jackdaw (Picture: Reuters) 
However, it has still faced strong criticism from environmental campaigners who say the gas extracted will ‘supercharge’ the climate crisis. 
Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, a joint venture between oil and gas giant Shell and the Norwegian state oil company Equinor. 
Adura boss Neil McCulloch said today’s decision ‘provides certainty to the businesses and skilled workers already delivering the project’. 
He is hoping approval is also given to Rosebank, since Adura plans to develop that oil field alongside Ithaca Energy. 
How will the Jackdaw decision affect my bills? 
Miatta Fahnbulleh was very careful to manage expectations in interviews this morning: this move will not bring down energy bills. 
She told LBC: ‘That was not a consideration in the decision because it won’t mean cheaper bills.’ 
The cost of the gas extracted from the Jackdaw field is determined by international prices, which have surged in recent years thanks to Russia’s war in Ukraine and disruption in the Gulf linked to the war in Iran.

articles.title: Estate records 'abundance' of wildlife despite drought
articles.raw_rss: Wimpole's "long-term approach to nature recovery" has seen more than 5,000 species recorded.

articles.jina_text:
A country house and farming estate in one of England's driest and most nature-depleted areas has an "abundance" of wildlife with more than 5,000 species recorded, the National Trust has said.
Rare species, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings, have been spotted at the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire in the last six years.
General manager David Hassall said the number was "remarkable in any landscape, but particularly here in Cambridgeshire, where wildlife is facing the combined pressures of habitat loss and increasingly hot, dry conditions".
The government said the East was one of seven UK areas in drought, with hosepipe bans in force across parts of the region.
The charity said 5,242 species were recorded across the estate's parkland, farmland, woodland and wetlands.
Hassall said the number "reflects five decades of careful stewardship and shows that nature can flourish alongside farming, public access and heritage conservation".

Press Association
The National Trust said it had recorded 5,242 species at Wimpole Estate in the last six years
Since 2021, the National Trust said it had planted 125,000 trees and created 35 hectares of woodland and 52 hectares of wood pasture, with another 77 hectares of tree planting currently being designed.





Advertisement












Species recorded also included a tiny pygmy ant, which the charity said was recorded at only one other UK site.
Ben McCarthy, head of nature conservation at the National Trust, said: "Across the UK, wildlife is under immense pressure from habitat loss and fragmentation as well as climate change, making the need to restore nature more urgent than ever.
"Places like Wimpole demonstrate the value of taking a long-term approach to nature recovery.
"By creating and restoring habitats across whole landscapes, we can provide more space for wildlife and help reverse decades of decline."
